grammar.label: negative scope and the words that need a negative to license them
grammar.form: any / ever / at all / budge / lift a finger, licensed by a preceding negative
grammar.meaning: explains why some words only appear in negative and question contexts

explanation.en: 'I have not seen anyone' is fine; 'I have seen anyone' is not. Certain words — any, ever, yet, at all, and idioms like 'lift a finger' — require a negative, a question or a doubting verb somewhere before them. The licence reaches forward, not back, which is why 'anyone did not come' fails while 'nobody came' works.
explanation.uz: 'I have not seen anyone' — to'g'ri; 'I have seen anyone' — xato. 'Any', 'ever', 'yet' kabi so'zlar oldidan inkor yoki savol talab qiladi. Ruxsat OLDINGA qarab ishlaydi, orqaga emas.

grammar.positive_example: Nobody has ever established who signed the second copy.
grammar.negative_example: Anybody has not ever established who signed the second copy.

l1_notes.uz: Rus tilida ikki karra inkor me'yoriy ('никто не пришёл'); ingliz tilida u xato, shuning uchun bu eng barqaror xatolardan biri.

grammar.label: focus particles and their scope — only, even, just, also
grammar.form: particle placed immediately before the element it focuses
grammar.meaning: decides which part of the sentence the particle is talking about

explanation.en: 'Only she told me on Tuesday' and 'she told only me on Tuesday' and 'she told me only on Tuesday' are three different claims. The particle focuses whatever follows it. Spoken English is forgiving because stress does the work; written English is not, and a misplaced 'only' is one of the commonest silent errors in careful prose.
explanation.uz: 'Only she told me on Tuesday', 'she told only me on Tuesday', 'she told me only on Tuesday' — uch xil ma'no. Zarracha o'zidan KEYINGI qismga ishora qiladi.

grammar.positive_example: The committee met only twice, and only after the deadline had passed.
grammar.negative_example: The committee only met twice, and only after the deadline had passed.

l1_notes.uz: O'zbek tilida 'faqat' odatda ta'kidlanayotgan so'z oldida turadi, shuning uchun qoida tanish; xato ingliz tilidagi odatdan kelib chiqadi.

body.speaker: Sarah
body.text: 'All of the districts did not reply.' Is that none, or some?

body.speaker: Sarah
body.text: Then you have written the opposite of what happened. 'Not all of the districts replied.'

body.speaker: Sarah
body.text: The order is not, and the order is the meaning. A lawyer would have a month's work out of that sentence.

body.speaker: Aziz
body.text: The next line says 'the committee only met twice'.

body.speaker: Sarah
body.text: Which tells me they only met and did not do anything else. Did they eat? Did they sleep?

body.speaker: Sarah
body.text: Now 'only' is next to the thing it is about. In speech your voice would have fixed it; on the page nothing will.

body.speaker: Aziz
body.text: And 'nobody has ever established who signed the second copy'?

body.speaker: Sarah
body.text: That is fine. 'Ever' needs a negative in front of it, and 'nobody' is doing that job.

body.speaker: Aziz
body.text: I wrote 'anybody has not ever established' in the first draft.

body.speaker: Sarah
body.text: Which is how Russian would let you do it, and English will not. The negative has to come first.
